'''Ronald Ward Hellings''' (23 January 1944 – 1 January 2022) was an American theoretical astrophysicist at [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] and [[Montana State University]], best known for the [[Hellings–Downs curve]] he co-derived with George Downs for detecting the [[stochastic gravitational wave background]] using [[pulsar timing array|pulsar timing arrays]]. Hellings' research focused on gravitational wave astronomy and astrophysical tests for [[Alternatives to general relativity|modifications to general relativity]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Backer |first=D. C. |last2=Hellings |first2=R. W. |date=1986 |title=Pulsar Timing and General Relativity |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.aa.24.090186.002541 |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |publisher=Annual Reviews |volume=24 |pages=537–575 |doi=10.1146/annurev.aa.24.090186.002541 |issn=1545-4282|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ron Hellings, Ph.D - Department of Physics {{!}} Montana State University |url=https://physics.montana.edu/directory/emeritus/hellings-ron.html |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=physics.montana.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Obituary information for Ronald Ward Hellings, Ph.D. |url=https://www.dokkennelson.com/obituaries/Ronald-Ward-Hellings-PhD?obId=23556871 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260511090208/https://www.dokkennelson.com/obituaries/Ronald-Ward-Hellings-PhD?obId=23556871 |archive-date=2026-05-11 |access-date=2026-09-08 |website=www.dokkennelson.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1983, Hellings and George Downs derived the [[Hellings–Downs curve]].

Hellings also sought to improve astrophysical constraints on deviations from general relativity. In response to a 1974 analysis of lunar motion by [[Tom Van Flandern]] which claimed to detect a decreasing [[gravitational constant]], in 1983 Hellings led an analysis of Earth-Mars distance data from [[Viking program|the Viking landers]] which found a null result in tension with Van Flandern.<ref>{{Cite journal |date= |title=A clock is a clock is a clock |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3968199 |journal=Science News |publisher=Society for Science & the Public, Wiley |volume=124 |issue=22 |pages=346–346 |doi=10.2307/3968199 |issn=0036-8423|year=1983|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Robinson |first=Arthur L. |date=1983 |title=New Test of Variable Gravitational Constant |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1691651 |journal=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |volume=222 |issue=4630 |pages=1316–1317 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kragh |first=Helge |title=Varying Gravity: Dirac's Legacy in Cosmology and Geophysics |date=2016 |publisher=Springer International Publishing : Imprint: Birkhäuser |isbn=978-3-319-24379-5 |edition=1st ed. 2016 |series=Science Networks. Historical Studies |location=Cham |pages=138-139 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-24379-5}}</ref> Hellings also used the Viking data to estimate the masses of Ceres, Pallas, and Vesta from their gravitational effects on Mars.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Murray |first=Carl |date=October 2013 |title=AskAstro |archive-url= |access-date= |pages=34 |volume=41 |issue=10|journal=Astronomy|via=2026-09-08|url=https://search.library.berkeley.edu/permalink/01UCS_BER/ppt38b/cdi_proquest_miscellaneous_1438672875}}</ref>

Hellings was the NASA program scientist for the [[Joint Dark Energy Mission]] proposal, which evolved into the [[Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Battersby |first=Stephen |date=2006-08-24 |title=Latecomer revs up dark energy race |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0262407906601942 |journal=New Scientist |volume=191 |issue=2564 |pages=8–9 |doi=10.1016/S0262-4079(06)60194-2 |issn=0262-4079|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
